claim: The combined use of specific viral serotype (either AAV2/1 or AAV2/9) and the human synapsin promoter resulted in almost exclusive GECI expression in somata and neurites of MLIs.
source: Although both MLIs and Purkinje cells (PCs) are PV positive, the combined use of specific viral serotype (either AAV2/1 or AAV2/9) and of the human synapsin promoter to drive expression, resulted in the almost exclusive GECI expression in somata and neurites of MLIs (Figure 1A; see also Kuhn et al., 2012; Astorga et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by references to prior work (Kuhn et al., 2012; Astorga et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1A showing expression pattern.

claim: Over 90% of MLIs expressed GECI as early as 7 days after injection.
source: On the other hand, the proportion of PV(+), CB(-) MLIs was very high (Figure 1B, right panel) with over 90% of MLIs expressing GECI as early as 7 days after injection.
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1B showing proportion of MLIs expressing GECI.

claim: The level of GCaMP expression increased during the first 2 weeks post-injection.
source: The level of expression increased during the first 2 weeks post-injection, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Temporal expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: High frequency PF stimulation generated robust Cai rises in MLIs expressing GCaMP3 proteins.
source: High frequency PF stimulation generated robust Cai rises in MLIs expressing GCaMP3 proteins and ΔF/Fo images displayed a characteristic beam-shaped increase in MLI fluorescence along the PF orientation (Sullivan et al., 2005; Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental observation with reference to Figure 1C showing beam-shaped fluorescence increases and citation to Sullivan et al., 2005.

claim: Increasing the train duration led to progressively larger peak Cai transients, with ΔF/Fo values increasing from 138.9 ± 30.6% for trains lasting 0.2 s to 347 ± 43% for 1 s long trains (N = 18).
source: Increasing the train duration led to progressively larger peak Cai transients, with ΔF/Fo values increasing from 138.9 ± 30.6% for trains lasting 0.2 s to 347 ± 43% for 1 s long trains (N = 18).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from 18 cells showing dose-response relationship.

claim: CPCCOEt significantly decreased peak amplitudes for the somatic signals in vivo.
source: We found that CPCCOEt significantly decreased peak amplitudes for the somatic signals in vivo (Figure 2A1, A2 and B3).
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation showing effect of mGluR1 antagonist with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The remaining Cai signal after CPCCOEt was abolished in all cases by adding a combination of non-competitive antagonists of AMPARs and NMDARs (GYKI53655 and DCK respectively), indicating the activation of iGluRs in MLIs.
source: The remaining Cai signal was abolished in all cases by adding a combination of non-competitive antagonists of AMPARs and NMDARs (GYKI53655 and DCK respectively; Figure 2B, yellow traces), indicating the activation of iGluRs in MLIs.
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing complete block by iGluR antagonists.

claim: The residual signal after CPCCOEt depended on AMPARs but not on NMDARs.
source: In two of the experiments DCK was added prior to GYKI53655; this failed to affect the CPCCOEt-insensitive Cai rises (example in Figure 2C), indicating that this residual signal depended on AMPARs but not on NMDARs.
evidence: Sequential pharmacological manipulation showing differential contribution of receptor types.

claim: Ratios of peak ΔF/Fo values in CPCCOEt over control in response to 1 s-long 100 Hz trains in vivo were similar to what was found in parallel experiments in slices.
source: On average, ratios of peak ΔF/Fo values in CPCCOEt over control in response to 1 s-long 100 Hz trains in vivo were similar to what we found in parallel experiments in slices (compare last two bars in Figure 2D; control peak ΔF/Fo was 347 ± 43% in vivo, n = 18; and 653 ± 58% in slices, n = 9), arguing for a strong contribution of mGluR1s in both cases.
evidence: Comparative quantitative data from in vivo and slice experiments.

claim: Analysis of in vivo Cai transients in the neuropil showed a significant reduction of peak Cai values by the mGluR1 antagonist, that was however smaller than the corresponding somatic reduction.
source: Analysis of in vivo Cai transients in the neuropil showed a significant reduction of peak Cai values by the mGluR1 antagonist, that was however smaller than the corresponding somatic reduction (ratio of ΔF/Fo in CPCCOEt to control values: 0.73 ± 0.03 in neuropil vs 0.47 ± 0,10 in somata; two-tailed p value from Wilcoxon test: 2.1 × 10−7).
evidence: Quantitative comparison between neuropil and somatic responses with statistical analysis.

claim: As the train duration was shortened the extent of block by CPCCOEt decreased, such that with a 100 ms train essentially no mGluR1 component was observed.
source: We found that as the train duration was shortened the extent of block decreased, such that with a 100 ms train essentially no mGluR1 component was observed (pooled data from 8 animals in Figure 2D).
evidence: Dose-response relationship from pooled data across 8 animals.

claim: A significant mGluR1 component was present only for the highest frequency tested (500 Hz) during 100 ms-long trains.
source: Pooled data analysis (Figure 2E) indicated that a significant mGluR1 component was present only for the highest frequency tested (500 Hz).
evidence: Frequency-response data from pooled analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Many of the identified cells exhibited fluorescence dynamics correlated to locomotion, with flat and low fluorescence during resting periods and increased fluorescence with temporal dynamics during locomotion periods.
source: Many of the identified cells exhibited fluorescence dynamics correlated to locomotion, that is, the fluorescence signal was flat and low during resting periods while it increased and showed temporal dynamics during locomotion periods (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observational data from awake behaving mice shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In control conditions, ΔF/Frest signals during locomotion had peak values of 128.2 ± 8.5% (313 ROIs from 4 mice).
source: In control conditions, ΔF/Frest signals during locomotion had peak values of 128.2 ± 8.5% (313 ROIs from 4 mice).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from 313 ROIs across 4 animals.

claim: A linear regression analysis on all the cells gave a correlation of −0.547 (R2 = 0.3, p<0.0001) meaning that a more probable decrease in Cai signal happened after CPCCOEt application if a higher fluorescence response was elicited during locomotion before drug application.
source: Indeed, a linear regression analysis on all the cells gave a correlation of −0.547 (R2 = 0.3, p<0.0001) meaning that a more probable decrease in Cai signal happened after CPCCOEt application if a higher fluorescence response was elicited during locomotion before drug application.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between pre-drug fluorescence and drug effect.

claim: Simultaneous addition of GYKI53655 and DCK strongly decreased PF-evoked Cai rises for all train durations tested in slices as well as in vivo.
source: We found that simultaneous addition of GYKI53655 and DCK (which together should abolish iGluR activation) strongly decreased PF-evoked Cai rises for all train durations tested in slices as well as in vivo (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation data from both in vivo and slice experiments.

claim: For a 100 Hz, 1 s long train, iGluR blockers blocked 94% of the response (ratio of drugs to control: 0.06 ± 0.01).
source: But the effect of iGluR block is much larger: for the same 100 Hz, 1 s long train the drugs block 94% of the response (ratio of drugs to control: 0.06 ± 0.01; Figure 4B).
evidence: Quantitative pharmacological data showing extent of block.

claim: IEM1460 had no effect on the PF-evoked Cai increases measured from the soma or the neuropil.
source: We found that this compound had no effect on the PF-evoked Cai increases measured from the soma or the neuropil (Figure 4C and D; ratios of control to IEM: 1.2 ± 0.05 and 1.0 ± 0.06 for 200 ms and 1 s trains at 100 Hz; n = 6 somas from 2 animals), suggesting a lack of Ca2+-permeability for AMPARs in MLIs of adult mice.
evidence: Pharmacological experiment with CP-AMPAR blocker showing no effect.

claim: All MLIs tested (n = 7) yielded linear I-V relations characteristic of Ca2+ impermeable AMPARs.
source: All MLIs tested (n = 7) yielded linear I-V relations characteristic of Ca2+ impermeable AMPARs (Cull-Candy et al., 2006; Figure 5B).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from 7 cells with reference to established criteria from Cull-Candy et al., 2006.

claim: AMPARs lose their Ca2+ permeability during development.
source: These data indicate that AMPARs lose their Ca2+ permeability during development, a developmental switch already reported for glutamatergic synapses in different brain regions (Kumar et al., 2002; Eybalin et al., 2004; Isaac et al., 2007).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior work showing similar developmental changes in other brain regions.

claim: Signals evoked in MLIs by glutamate uncaging had peak ΔF/Fo values of 342 ± 47% (n = 12) in control saline and 5 ± 3% (n = 10) in the presence of CPCCOEt, showing that they were mediated by mGluR1.
source: Signals evoked in MLIs by glutamate uncaging had peak ΔF/Fo values of 342 ± 47% (n = 12) in control saline and 5 ± 3% (n = 10) in the presence of CPCCOEt, showing that they were mediated by mGluR1.
evidence: Quantitative pharmacological data from glutamate uncaging experiments.

claim: mGluR1-induced Cai rises were strongly decreased by addition of CdCl2 to the extracellular solution, with peak ΔF/Fo decreasing from 438 ± 47% to 6 ± 2% (n = 4).
source: We found that these Cai rises were strongly decreased by addition of CdCl2 to the extracellular solution (Figure 5C and D). On average, peak ΔF/Fo decreased from 438 ± 47% to 6 ± 2% (n = 4).
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation with voltage-gated calcium channel blocker.

claim: iGluRs act on the mGluR1-induced response via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: These results indicate that iGluRs acts on the mGluR1-induced response via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
evidence: Interpretation based on the CdCl2 blocking experiment.

claim: Strong mGluR1α immunoreactivity has been described for all GABAergic neurons in the cerebellar cortex.
source: We used an mGluR1α antibody because strong mGluR1α immunoreactivity has been described for all GABAergic neurons in the cerebellar cortex (Baude et al., 1993) while no immunoreactivity has been found in MLIs for other mGluR1 isoforms (mGluR1b and mGluR1c) (Grandes et al., 1994).
evidence: Cited from prior immunohistochemical studies.

claim: No immunoreactivity has been found in MLIs for other mGluR1 isoforms (mGluR1b and mGluR1c).
source: We used an mGluR1α antibody because strong mGluR1α immunoreactivity has been described for all GABAergic neurons in the cerebellar cortex (Baude et al., 1993) while no immunoreactivity has been found in MLIs for other mGluR1 isoforms (mGluR1b and mGluR1c) (Grandes et al., 1994).
evidence: Cited from prior immunohistochemical study.

claim: mGluR1α are remarkably close to the PSD, with the highest density occurring within the first 50 nm from the edge of the synapse.
source: This analysis showed that mGluR1α are remarkably close to the PSD, with the highest density occurring within the first 50 nm from the edge of the synapse (Figure 6C).
evidence: Quantitative electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: mGluR1s are ideally located to engage in synergistic interactions with AMPARs following the release of glutamate by presynaptic PFs.
source: Thus, mGluR1s are ideally located to engage in synergistic interactions with AMPARs following the release of glutamate by presynaptic PFs.
evidence: Interpretation based on the spatial proximity data from electron microscopy.

claim: mGluR1s are activated in vivo by synaptically-released glutamate both during electrical stimulation of PFs in anesthetized mice and during enforced locomotion in awake mice.
source: Firstly, we show that mGluR1s are activated in vivo by synaptically-released glutamate both during electrical stimulation of PFs in anesthetized mice and during enforced locomotion in awake mice.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from both anesthetized and awake experiments.

claim: The relative contribution of mGluR1 activation to the postsynaptic Cai signals increases sharply as a function of the duration of presynaptic action potential trains.
source: Furthermore, we show that the relative contribution of mGluR1 activation to the postsynaptic Cai signals increases sharply as a function of the duration of presynaptic action potential trains.
evidence: Summary of dose-response findings from electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: Activation of mGluR1s and iGluRs act in synergy to produce Cai rises.
source: Secondly, we show that activation of mGluR1s and iGluRs act in synergy to produce Cai rises.
evidence: Summary of pharmacological findings showing synergistic interaction.

claim: The spatial distribution of mGluR1s and iGluRs at the PF-MLI synapse favors iGluR/mGluR1 synergy following homosynaptic receptor activation.
source: Third, we show that the spatial distribution of these receptors at the PF-MLI synapse, as revealed by quantitative EM, favors iGluR/mGluR1 synergy following homosynaptic receptor activation.
evidence: Summary of electron microscopy findings showing receptor proximity.

claim: High frequency trains of PF activity, resembling sensory input to the cerebellar cortex and spike bursts recorded from granule cells in vivo during somatosensory peripheral stimulation, engage mGluR1s depending on the activation of iGluRs.
source: We further show that high frequency trains of PF activity, resembling sensory input to the cerebellar cortex and spike bursts recorded from granule cells (GCs) in vivo during somatosensory peripheral stimulation (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006), engage mGluR1s depending on the activation of iGluRs.
evidence: Experimental findings with reference to physiologically relevant activity patterns from Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006.

claim: mGluR1-dependent Cai signaling has been observed before in vivo following beam activation of PFs, but this signal may have been indirect as it had a latency >10 s.
source: While mGluR1-dependent Cai signaling has been observed before in vivo following beam activation of PFs (Wang et al., 2011), this signal may have been indirect as it had a latency >10 s; furthermore, its cellular origin remained uncertain, even though it was suggested that the primary signal source was PCs.
evidence: Citation to prior work with critical evaluation of its interpretation.

claim: The present work indicates direct mGluR1 activation at PF-MLI synapses with a latency well below 1 s.
source: By contrast, our work indicates direct mGluR1 activation at PF-MLI synapses with a latency well below 1 s.
evidence: Comparison of current findings to prior work, emphasizing faster kinetics.

claim: mGluR1 activation in vivo may be a widespread phenomenon, occurring under a variety of morphologically different synapses, and following common presynaptic activity patterns.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that mGluR1 activation in vivo may be a widespread phenomenon, occurring under a variety of morphologically different synapses, and following common presynaptic activity patterns.
evidence: Generalization based on findings at PF-MLI synapses which lack ensheathing elements.

claim: The activation of MLIs during locomotion is expected as recordings were in lobule IV/V of the cerebellar vermis which encodes fore- and hindlimb sensory-motor information.
source: The activation of MLIs during locomotion reported here is expected as we recorded in lobule IV/V of the cerebellar vermis which encodes fore- and hindlimb sensory-motor information (Provini et al., 1968; Buisseret-Delmas and Angaut, 1993).
evidence: Interpretation based on known functional anatomy cited from prior work.

claim: Both electrical activity and activity-dependent Cai signals in MLIs increase during locomotion.
source: It is in accord with recent work showing that both electrical activity (Jelitai et al., 2016) and activity-dependent Cai signals in MLIs increase during locomotion (Ozden et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from recent prior studies on MLI activity during locomotion.

claim: During locomotion, a vast majority of GCs are activated, with 94% of all GCs in a large field of view being activated according to Ozden et al. (2012).
source: During locomotion, likewise, a vast majority of GCs are activated, 94% of all GCs in a large field of view, according to Ozden et al. (2012) and the impact on MLIs is a change in firing rate from an average value of 20 Hz in quiet mice to 60 Hz during self-paced locomotion (Jelitai et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited quantitative data from prior studies on GC and MLI activity.

claim: GC firing in mice walking spontaneously occurs in high frequency bursts with instantaneous frequencies within a burst ranging from 60 to 142 Hz, and burst durations ranging from 30 to 140 ms.
source: In time, firing occurs in high frequency bursts with instantaneous frequencies within a burst ranging from 60 to 142 Hz, and burst durations ranging from 30 to 140 ms.
evidence: Description of physiological firing patterns, likely from cited literature or general knowledge.

claim: The values of GC burst frequencies and durations during spontaneous walking are close to those needed to obtain measurable mGluR responses with extracellular stimulation.
source: Strikingly, these values are close to those needed to obtain measurable mGluR responses with extracellular stimulation (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison between physiological activity patterns and experimental stimulation parameters.

claim: The correlation between the extent of mGluR1 block and the Cai rise amplitude may arise from different patterns of PF activity during the behaviors.
source: The correlation between the extent of block and the Cai rise amplitude may arise from different patterns of PF activity during the behaviors.
evidence: Interpretation of the correlation data from locomotion experiments.

claim: High frequency or prolonged PF activity will induce strong Cai rises in MLIs through the synergy between iGluRs and mGluR.
source: High frequency or prolonged PF activity will induce strong Cai rises in MLIs through the synergy between iGluRs and mGluR.
evidence: Summary statement integrating experimental findings.

claim: The synergy between iGluRs and mGluR1 works as a nonlinear switch, gating the plasticity at PF-MLI synapses and governing the inhibition output of MLIs.
source: This synergy works as a nonlinear switch, gating the plasticity at PF-MLI synapses and governing the inhibition output of MLIs.
evidence: Functional interpretation of the synergistic mechanism.

claim: In slices, the response of MLIs to mGluR1 agonists is abolished by removal of external Ca2+ ions or by inclusion of the VGCC blocker Cd2+.
source: In slices, the response of MLIs to mGluR1 agonists is abolished by removal of external Ca2+ ions (Collin et al., 2009) or by inclusion of the VGCC blocker Cd2+ (this work).
evidence: Combination of cited prior work and current experimental data.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ entry is necessary for mGluR1-activated Cai rises.
source: This shows that voltage-gated Ca2+ entry is necessary for mGluR1-activated Cai rises.
evidence: Conclusion from pharmacological experiments blocking VGCCs.

claim: AMPAR activation provides a depolarization that activates VGCCs, thus initiating the Cai rise and bootstrapping the mGluR1-activated response.
source: In this context, our in vivo results showing that mGluR1-dependent rises are totally dependent on simultaneous iGluR activation strongly suggest that AMPAR activation provides a depolarization that activates VGCCs, thus initiating the Cai rise and bootstrapping the mGluR1-activated response.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation based on pharmacological dependence data.

claim: AMPARs alone are responsible for the synergy with mGluR1.
source: Although most of our experiments used both AMPAR and NMDAR blockers, the evidence shown in Figure 2 indicates that AMPARs alone are responsible for the synergy.
evidence: Interpretation based on sequential pharmacological experiments in Figure 2.

claim: AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy at PF-PC synapses is in accordance with the reliance of mGluR1-dependent IP3 production on AMPAR activation.
source: This is in accordance with the reliance of mGluR1-dependent IP3 production on AMPAR activation at PF-PC synapses (Okubo et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison to prior findings in Purkinje cells.

claim: A plausible source for the synergistic nature of the signals is the Ca2+-dependence of phospholipase C, which has been documented in cerebellar PCs.
source: A plausible source for the synergistic nature of the signals is the Ca2+-dependence of phospholipase C, which has been documented in cerebellar PCs (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis based on cited prior work on PLC.

claim: AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy constitutes a double key system controlling postsynaptic Cai responses following prolonged PF stimulation.
source: Taken together these results suggest that AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy constitutes a double key system controlling postsynaptic Cai responses following prolonged PF stimulation.
evidence: Conceptual summary of the synergistic mechanism.

claim: The double key control of AMPAR/mGluR1 is analogous to the well-documented joined requirement for AMPAR and NMDAR activation in the induction of long-term synaptic plasticity.
source: This double key control is analogous to the well-documented joined requirement for AMPAR and NMDAR activation in the induction of long-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Analogy to established mechanisms in synaptic plasticity.

claim: NMDARs are present extrasynaptically in MLIs.
source: Interestingly, while NMDARs are present extrasynaptically in MLIs (Carter and Regehr, 2000; Clark and Cull-Candy, 2002), the PF-MLI synapses lack NMDARs (Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Clark and Cull-Candy, 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: PF-MLI synapses lack NMDARs.
source: Interestingly, while NMDARs are present extrasynaptically in MLIs (Carter and Regehr, 2000; Clark and Cull-Candy, 2002), the PF-MLI synapses lack NMDARs (Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Clark and Cull-Candy, 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: PF-MLI synapses are the site of various forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: Nevertheless, PF-MLI synapses are the site of various forms of synaptic plasticity (reviewed by Dean et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from review article.

claim: The combined activation of AMPARs and mGluR1s at PF-MLI synapses could control the rise of a postsynaptic calcium signal responsible for associative synaptic plasticity.
source: The combined activation of AMPARs and mGluR1s at PF-MLI synapses could control the rise of a postsynaptic calcium signal responsible for associative synaptic plasticity, similarly to the combined activation of AMPARs and NMDARs in other synapses.
evidence: Hypothesis about functional role in plasticity by analogy to other systems.

claim: In a subset of interneurons in the hippocampus, a form of long-term synaptic plasticity requires simultaneous activation of mGluR1s, of Ca2+-permeant AMPARs, and of T-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Likewise, in a subset of interneurons in the hippocampus, a form of long-term synaptic plasticity requires simultaneous activation of mGluR1s, of Ca2+-permeant AMPARs, and of T-type Ca2+ channels (Nicholson and Kullmann, 2017).
evidence: Cited from prior work on hippocampal interneurons.

claim: There is another form of synergy between iGluRs and mGluRs involving the electrical field induced by activation of iGluRs, which retards the escape of charged glutamate from the synaptic cleft and favors the activation of mGluRs.
source: Interestingly, there is another form of synergy between iGluRs and mGluRs involving the electrical field induced by activation of iGluRs, which retards the escape of charged glutamate from the synaptic cleft and favors the activation of mGluRs (Sylantyev et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited alternative mechanism from prior work.

claim: The electrical field mechanism alone is unlikely to account for the observed synergy, because this synergy depends on Ca2+ influx.
source: Our data does not allow us to exclude this possibility, but this phenomenon alone is unlikely to account for the observed synergy, because this synergy depends on Ca2 influx.
evidence: Reasoning based on the Ca2+ dependence of the observed synergy.

claim: PF-PC synapses are located on PC spines while PF-MLI synapses occur on smooth MLI dendrites.
source: PF-PC synapses are located on PC spines while PF-MLI synapses occur on smooth MLI dendrites.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar synapses.

claim: PF-PC synapses are encapsulated with glia, thus preventing neurotransmitter escape, whereas PF-MLI synapses lack ensheathing elements.
source: Furthermore, PF-PC synapses are encapsulated with glia, thus preventing neurotransmitter escape, whereas PF-MLI synapses lack ensheathing elements.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar synapses.

claim: The location of mGluR1α on PF-PC synapses was found to be perisynaptic, with 50% of mGluR1α particles located within 60 nm of the edge of the synapse.
source: As in the present work, the location of mGluR1α on PF-PC synapses was found to be perisynaptic (Baude et al., 1993; Lujan et al., 1996; Luján et al., 1997), and it was calculated that 50% of mGluR1α particles were located within 60 nm of the edge of the synapse.
evidence: Cited quantitative data from prior EM studies on Purkinje cells.

claim: The percentage of mGluR1α within 60 nm of the synapse edge in PF-PC synapses is close to the value reported for MLIs.
source: This percentage is close to the value reported here for MLIs.
evidence: Comparison between current findings and prior work on PCs.

claim: The close association of mGluR1s with the PSD rim in both PF-PC and PF-MLI synaptic types is consistent with the AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy.
source: The close association of mGluR1s with the PSD rim in both synaptic types is consistent with the AMPAR/mGluR1 synergy proposed above.
evidence: Interpretation linking structural and functional findings.

claim: The spatial arrangement of mGluR1s strongly suggests that in both PF-PC and PF-MLI synapses, mGluR1 activation primarily results from homosynaptic glutamate release, and not from glutamate spillover.
source: In addition, this spatial arrangement strongly suggests that in both cases, mGluR1 activation primarily results from homosynaptic glutamate release, and not from glutamate spillover.
evidence: Interpretation based on receptor proximity to release sites.

claim: The PSD size for PF-MLI synapses is twice smaller than that of PF-PC synapses.
source: The PSD size for PF-MLI synapses is twice smaller than that of PF-PC synapses (Abrahamsson et al., 2012), and this results in a significantly shorter distance between the site of vesicular release and mGluR1s, favoring homosynaptic activation of mGluR1s.
evidence: Cited anatomical data with functional interpretation.

claim: The absence of a diffusion barrier imposed by glial membranes around the PF-MLI synapse and a lower density of glutamate transporter proteins would seem to favor activation by synaptic cross-talk in PF-MLI synapses.
source: On the other hand, while glial covering and glutamate uptake favor synapse isolation and hence homosynaptic signaling in PF-PC synapses, the absence of a diffusion barrier imposed by glial membranes around the PF-MLI synapse (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974), and a lower density of glutamate transporter proteins (Chaudhry et al., 1995), would seem to favor activation by synaptic cross-talk in PF-MLI synapses.
evidence: Cited anatomical features with functional interpretation.

claim: The advantage of the short distance between release sites and mGluR1s overrules the disadvantage of the lack of glial covering, so that overall, homosynaptic activation prevails also in the case of the PF-MLI synapse.
source: Nevertheless, the present finding of a close association of mGluR1 to the PSD at PF-MLI synapses suggests that the advantage of the short distance overrules the disadvantage of the lack of glial covering, so that overall, homosynaptic activation prevails also in the case of the PF-MLI synapse.
evidence: Interpretation weighing competing factors affecting glutamate signaling.

claim: Compared to AMPARs, mGluR1s display slow activation kinetics and low desensitization rates.
source: Compared to AMPARs, mGluR1s display slow activation kinetics and low desensitization rates.
evidence: Established biophysical properties of receptor types.

claim: Single synaptic release results in a small number of activated mGluR1 receptors.
source: Consequently, single synaptic release results in a small number of activated receptors.
evidence: Inference from the slow kinetics of mGluR1s.

claim: A few pulses of high frequency release can recruit a sufficient number of mGluR1s to trigger a measurable response as observed in slice experiments for PF-PC synapses and for PF-MLI synapses.
source: A few pulses of high frequency release, however, can recruit a sufficient number of mGluR1s to trigger a measurable response as observed in slice experiments for PF-PC synapses (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998) and for PF-MLI synapses (Karakossian and Otis, 2004).
evidence: Cited from prior slice electrophysiology studies.

claim: Longer stimulation trains are expected to recruit an increasing proportion of mGluR1s as their activation develops further while AMPAR desensitization occurs.
source: Longer stimulation trains are expected to recruit an increasing proportion of mGluR1s as their activation develops further while AMPAR desensitization occurs.
evidence: Prediction based on known receptor kinetics.

claim: The in vivo results show a growing contribution of mGluR1s to PF-induced Cai responses as a function of train duration, in line with the expectation from receptor kinetics.
source: Our in vivo results are in line with this expectation, showing a growing contribution of mGluR1s to PF-induced Cai responses as a function of train duration.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings confirming predictions.

claim: mGluR1-mediated Cai rises start to be observed for bursts of PF activity lasting about 100 ms, a duration commonly recorded in vivo during sensory input or behavior.
source: We start seeing mGluR1-mediated Cai rises for bursts of PF activity lasting about 100 ms, a duration commonly recorded in vivo during sensory input or behavior (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006).
evidence: Experimental threshold determination with reference to physiological activity patterns.

claim: The actual threshold for activation of mGluR1 in vivo is probably somewhat lower than the 100 ms estimate due to limitations of GCaMP-based signals compared to organic Ca2+ dyes.
source: Given the above slice results, and because our GCaMP-based signals do not have the same resolution as signals reported by organic Ca2+ dyes, it is probable that the actual threshold for activation of mGluR1 in vivo is somewhat lower than our 100 ms estimate.
evidence: Caveat about measurement limitations affecting threshold estimate.
